What does that mean?

In the world of neuroimaging, which is where I come from,
there are terms that get tossed around a lot: "networks",
"circuits", "computational model".
And that's true.
I mean, these are real entities.
These are important areas of research
that have yielded really important insights.
But different fields have different ways
of understanding the same words.
And so for the sake of clarity, I
want to be kind of clear about what
we mean by these things in this context.
In the context of neuroimaging,
when we say "networks", and even sometimes "circuits",
what is typically meant is something
that looks like this, where we have a seed region,
and then we're asking, what other areas of the brain
are co-activated with that seed region?
So what we're really doing is taking a time series
from one region and asking for the time series that
are obtained from every other voxel in the brain
or every other region in the brain,
depending on how you parsellate your brain.
The areas that are associated with that first region that
are somehow connected or communicating or signaling
are described in that way based on correlation coefficients.
You can also expand this to a general linear model, where
you have a design matrix and you ask,
in response to some particular experimental input: what areas
are activated in response to that input, differentially,
let's say, between one condition versus another,
between one population versus another?
But these are all statistical tests.
When we talk about computational modeling or computational
neuroscience within the neuroimaging world, what
is often meant is really something very,
very different than how basic neuroscientists would think
of computational neuroscience.
What's happening [in neuroimaging] is that there is an emphasis, really,
on developing tools that are able to make
better use of the time series that
are obtained from these voxels.
The sorts of computational tools that
have been developed in neuroimaging,
by and large (there are exceptions),
really, they hinge around two different concepts.
One is improving reliability and reproducibility of connectivity,
which as we said, are correlations,
co-activation patterns, which are described
through the general linear model, or feature extraction,
often through independent components
analysis using meta analyses across data sets and modalities.
Given what has sometimes been described
as a reproducibility crisis within the fMRI world,
there's a very strong effort to see, OK,
if we say these networks exist for one data set,
do they also exist for other data sets?
If we say they exist for fMRI, can we
elicit them also from MEG?
So the idea here is really to use computational power
to enhance this reproducibility and reliability.
The second context is using some methods
from machine learning to decode functions and disorders
from time series.
And in this case, what's really happening
is that people are identifying signatures, brain signatures,
for this disorder versus that disorder,
or for this function versus that function.
And here, the advantage is that decoding actually
can be done not just on time series,
but on lots of different types of data.
So you can use multimodal data and use structural information,
functional information, all sorts of information
together to provide these sorts of diagnostic tools.
But for the purposes of what I've said in terms of our aims,
those two approaches are not what we mean
by computational neuroscience.
For one thing, what we need is
to be able to simulate the impact of one drug
or device versus another, to tune parameters
and ask how the system will change, to ask how a patient who
has undergone deep brain stimulation
is likely to respond to tuning parameters
this way versus that way.
All of this requires simulation.
This requires an element of time.
So it's not just asking: are you in this category
or this category?
It's asking: how does the system evolve over time?
Both of these methods that I've described
are discriminative.
You can't simulate with them.
You can describe symptoms.
You can describe disorders.
You can describe functions.
But what you can't do is simulate
how they will evolve over time.
In terms of interpretability, machine learning
has its strengths precisely because it's high dimensional
in this context.
There are types of machine learning,
of course, that are generative.
But that's not what's being generally applied
to neuroimaging data.
But because it's high dimensional,
the flip side to that is that it's not interpretable.
So you can't take those signatures elicited
by machine learning from neuroimaging data
and then reverse engineer what actually the brain is doing.
Likewise, using multiple pairwise correlations
to infer circuit architecture is not very reliable
when you're looking at networks.
For one thing, circuits include feedback,
and correlations fall apart when you're
looking at systems that include feedback.
The second point is that in a network,
you have pairwise correlations, which
if you add them-- so if you have a particular network with nodes
and you ask, what's the correlation between this node
and this node, and then this node and this node,
and this node and this node, the error estimates for each edge
multiply.
And as a result, when you ask, what
is the error of a single connection,
the error for a single connection
might be totally manageable.
But once you get to a network with many edges,
you have this exponential amplification of error.
It can very quickly get out of control.
And actually, if you start with an R value, so a Pearson
correlation of 0.45, which is quite
strong within neuroimaging, you'd
be super happy if you got such a correlation.
But that's only explaining 20% of the variance, which
means 80% of the variance is not being explained.
Now, if you have three steps, you
have 0.2 cubed, which means that you're not explaining
over 99% of the variance.
That's not a very good model.
So for that reason, it's not a great way
to identify the structure of circuits.
The other problem is that even if you
were doing a great job of absolutely identifying
the structure of the circuit with your networks,
the other issue is that just talking
about who's connected to whom is a very
sparse amount of information about the structure
of your model.
And so as we'll see, there are a lot
of functions, really critical functions within the brain, that
require a lot more information than who is talking to whom.
So if that's not what we're using,
if we're not going to be just relying on connectivity,
connectivity understood as correlation coefficients
or general linear models, then what we'll be using
is something called dynamical systems,
which are based on ODE systems.
The advantage of ODE systems is
that they address a lot of the concerns that I just raised.
You can talk about the error of the system
as a whole in a way that you can't with a series
of correlations.
You can model explicitly feedback
and also, you can simulate.
And so here, I take as a really simple example glucose insulin
regulation.
This is something that probably all of you know about.
You eat a cookie.
Your glucose levels go up.
But glucose levels being too high is quite dangerous.
And so your endocrine system has a feedback loop that
allows you to release insulin.
Insulin then lowers your glucose levels.
If your glucose levels go too low, then you release glucagon
and the glucose levels go up.
So here you have a homeostatic regulatory system
that maintains glucose within appropriate thresholds.
And so what you can see here is if we give a glucose bolus,
we can simulate how glucose and insulin will respond.
So glucose will respond first.
Insulin will respond shortly thereafter.
And then glucose will go down.
And then insulin will go down.
You can see that one of the nice features of this kind of model
is that if we say that the circuit is dysregulated,
we can be kind of precise about how it gets dysregulated.
And it turns out that different ways
of dysregulating the same circuit
will lead to very different phenotypes.
In Type 1 diabetes, unmedicated Type 1 diabetics
tend to be very, very thin because insulin
is responsible for putting on body fat and storing it.
Type 2 diabetics who are unmedicated
will tend to be overweight because they
have too much insulin, and they're storing the glucose
rather than consuming it.
So if you were to just look at individuals with Type 1 and Type
2 diabetes and just look at those phenotypes,
you wouldn't necessarily understand
that those two disorders, which look completely different
from a clinical perspective, actually
represent different types of dysregulation
of the very same circuit.
That is actually kind of provocative
when we think about psychiatric disorders,
because psychiatric disorders tend
to implicate many of the same circuits, in spite of the fact
that [their clinical presentations] can look quite different.
And so this provides a way of thinking
for how that might occur.
Importantly, also, I've just done a hypothetical experiment
here.
I've given glucose.
I've seen how there's a response over time.
But what's very nice about being able to simulate
is I can ask, all right, if we chronically do this,
how will the system change over time?
We can ask about longer term trajectories.
So when we do experiments in the lab,
whether we're doing it in the scanner
or we're doing it with electrophysiology,
we have a very small time window in which
we can conduct our experiments.
But clinically, disorders, diseases, they evolve sometimes
over decades.
And so understanding how that process occurs
is something that we can do with simulations.
One example here is with Type 2 diabetes.
If there's a chronically elevated demand for insulin,
beta cells hit their carrying capacity.
After a certain point, the beta cells, they're fatigued.
They can't keep up with the demand.
And as a result, Type 2 diabetics can also become Type
1-like diabetics.
Again, this provides a way of thinking
about certain types of psychiatric disorders
that seem to flip states, so for example, from mania
to depression, all sorts of states from anxiety
to depression.
There are all sorts of trajectory changes
that occur over much longer periods of time
than you can measure in a laboratory
that you'd want to be able to explain
with your computational models.
And note that when I say carrying capacity,
in the context of neuroscience, this is a very real concern,
because a lot of these dysregulations
are putting a tremendous amount of excess stress on the system.
And so if you are in a state, like mania, where you're rapidly
depleting dopamine, then what you're going to do
is to put a lot of stress on precursors for dopamine,
like tyrosine, for example, where acetylcholine
has a precursor choline.
And what can happen is that as you hit that carrying capacity,
the system can collapse.
This is a really important dynamic, overshoot and collapse,
that you'll want to be keeping in mind for the models.
